data.title: Why Advent calendars are thriving in the ‘little treat’ economy
data.description: The countdown to Christmas began in October — at least on social media. Over the past few months, content creators have been getting a head start on the holidays by unboxing, reviewing and promoting an array of Advent calendars. The anticipation behind each cardboard flap has translated into millions of views, as consumers lean into the surge in popularity surrounding the product. “Brands are bringing out their advent calendars earlier and earlier, and so they go faster every year,” said TikTok creator Courtney Cahoon, who said nowadays she’s purchasing the calendars as early as August and sharing highlights with her 1.7 million followers. The calendars originated in Germany in the 20th century, where a printer took inspiration from the candies attached to cardboard he had used to count down to Christmas as a child, according to retail giant Williams Sonoma. While the calendars are not a new holiday offering, demand for the product has increased in recent years — which explains why it might feel like there’s a calendar for just about everything and for just about everyone. Global market for such calendars could reach $2.47 billion by 2033, according to trade publication Retail Insider. Nowadays, the calendars have evolved into a marketing vehicle for brands looking to showcase everything from everyday essentials like McCormick’s spices to luxury goods like a $1,020 set of mini perfumes from Maison Francis Kurkdijan. Experts like Freddy Tran Nager, an associate professor of communication at the University of Southern California, attribute the popularity of the calendars to what’s called “the treat economy.” “We’ve had a rough few years,” said Nager, the founder of the marketing consultancy Atomic Tango LLC, referring to the economic challenges facing the U.S. economy. “And so you know, some people indulge in what’s called the ‘treat economy.’ They can’t afford a car. They can’t afford a home, but they can certainly afford little treats for themselves.” Creators who specialize in sharing product recommendations on their feeds — sometimes in exchange for a commission from the brands — have also encouraged users to lean into indulging in calendar deals earlier and earlier. On platforms like TikTok, searches for “advent calendar” spiked from Nov. 2-8, with the app reporting that many of its creators have posted videos sharing which calendars are underrated and which offer the best value. Ahead of Black Friday, TikTok said in a recent weekly trends report that more “creators are sharing holiday gift guides and reviewing advent calendars. Shoppers are also turning to TikTok Shop for holiday finds.” Faire, an online wholesale platform that tracks consumer habits, told NBC News in an email that “by the end of September, retailers had already spent more on advent calendars than in all of last season.” Hannah Wall, Faire’s trend expert, also attributed to the popularity of the advent calendar to “treat culture,” citing peak interest from Gen Z. “Gen Z has made it an adult staple because it’s the ultimate small treat and they’re choosing squishies, tea, jam, and beauty countdowns over chocolate for a daily dose of holiday joy,” Wall wrote in an email statement. Jintao Zhang, an assistant professor of marketing at Binghamton University, offered a similar observation. “We know that the largest consumer group consuming social media is Gen Z,” he said, adding that the age group “determines the prevalence and also the attractiveness of advent calendar on social media.” Social media users also tend to trust content creators, particularly those with smaller followings who are known as “micro” or “nano” influencers, according to Zhang. Still, he warned people to be cautious as some influencers post content that is sponsored without necessarily disclosing it in an obvious way. Influencers typically approach their calendar videos in two different ways: Some do countdowns, going through each day of the calendar individually (as intended); while others open an entire calendar in one video, sharing its contents altogether. Natalie Violette, a beauty and lifestyle influencer with more than 4 million followers on TikTok, said she either purchases or receives the calendars from brands in an effort to maintain authenticity in her reviews. “They like seeing … the honest reactions and reviews on these calendars, and definitely … the surprise factor, no question, I think that’s what really brings them in,” said Violette, whose journey with this type of content began three years ago when a follower challenged her to do a complete makeup look just by using products from a calendar. Her calendar videos have become so popular that they draw in new viewers every holiday season. The calendars she posts often sell out, she added. Even calendars that she isn’t a fan of pick up traction online. For example, Violette was among the creators who criticized the Skims calendar, which, for $148, included hair ties and bobby pins. As a result of the online backlash, the Kim Kardashian-owned brand began offering refunds to customers who were unhappy with the product. Sarah Lynn, who has built a following of more than 200,000 followers on TikTok for her calendar content, described it as “super fun” to show people what’s on the market. Sometimes, however, she said the offerings are hit or miss. She particularly doesn’t appreciate when brands are “just filling it with random kinds of junk that they know are not really their best selling products.” “If this was not my job and if this wasn’t what I was doing for work, I would not be spending all this money,” Lynn said. “But I never want people to feel like they have to buy anything or that they’re necessarily missing out.” “Whatever people want to take from my content, they can definitely take from it,” she added. “Whether it’s entertainment or shopping inspiration or neither.”

data.title: Cautious consumers gear up for Black Friday as inflation woes bite
data.description: NEW YORK/LOS ANGELES — Neither high fuel prices nor stubborn inflation are expected to stop U.S. shoppers from spending robustly as ​their turkey hangovers wear off on Black Friday. But below healthy top-line forecasts lie signs of stress. Holiday spending — which unofficially begins on ‌Black Friday — is seen topping last year’s strong figures by 4%-6%, several economic forecasts show. But most of the gains will be attributable to inflation which, at 3.8%, is about a percentage point higher than in each of the last two years. The National Retail Federation sees November-December holiday retail sales rising 4.2% year-over-year, to just above $1 trillion. The Mastercard Economics Institute and EY Parthenon ​each forecast sales to rise more than 5%. Eventual final results often beat pre-holiday estimates. Still, consumer sentiment remains shaky. This month, voters punished President ​Donald Trump for an Iran War that’s pushed the cost of living higher, handing Democrats sweeping electoral victories. A November survey by ⁠the National Retail Federation found that 82% of consumers are taking steps to manage holiday costs, like buying less expensive gifts. Los Angeles resident Felicia Cox, 50, said ​that while her holiday spending will be roughly stable, inflation is impacting how she thinks. “I want to get more gifts that people will actually use or need,” said ​Cox, a sales representative, while browsing in an L.A. Marshalls last week. “I feel like people aren’t able to afford as much stuff.” Worries aside, some 87% of 1,200 consumers surveyed by Deloitte in October planned to participate in the five-day shopping period from Thanksgiving through “Cyber Monday,” November 30 — the highest in a decade, according to Deloitte. “People like to spend during the holidays,” even ​when there’s a “persisting undercurrent of stress,” said Katie Thomas, who leads the Kearney Consumer Institute, part of global consulting firm Kearney. Middle- and lower-income shoppers — who have ​been trading down for months — were however more likely than wealthy ones to spend less, according to the Kearney survey. Target, Dollar Tree and Kohl’s have all pointed to belt-tightening during recent ‌earnings calls. ⁠Kohl’s CEO Michael Bender on Tuesday cited an “increasingly choiceful” consumer that is “looking to stretch every dollar.” Holiday spending forecasts mostly predated the recent stock market correction that followed the midterms, turmoil at chipmaker Nvidia, and mounting concerns around an AI bubble. The decline could dampen the wealth effect that has seen affluent shoppers splurge on gadgets and accessories, UBS analysts said in a note on Tuesday. Toys take a hit Higher input costs, particularly from petrol derivatives like plastic, are hitting some products more than others. Prices of ​toys — generally high in plastic — have risen ​13.2% since the start of the ⁠year, pushing Barbie maker Mattel this month to cut its annual forecast as consumers balked at higher costs. Some unlikely products are buoying the toy category. Best Buy and Target have both flagged trading cards — including Pokemon and Magic: The Gathering products — as a key ​growth driver. Squishy NeeDoh toys were selling for $24.99 on Amazon in October, nearly triple the price a year earlier ​on hot demand, according ⁠to e-commerce marketing platform Omnisend. Toy maker Learning Resources Inc — a plaintiff in lawsuits that overturned Trump’s tariffs — is seeing demand roughly flat, said CEO Rick Woldenberg, though he added it’s hard to predict demand before Black Friday. “People can’t shop until they have their turkey,” Woldenberg said. AI could also scramble the year’s shopping dynamics. As shoppers use AI ⁠to find bargains ​or even complete purchases — and retailers become increasingly adept at altering price quickly through AI — the deepest ​discounts could come closer to Christmas, as consumers and retailers both wait out the market, said Ryan Orabone, a consultant at Spaulding Ridge. “My advice to shoppers is to be patient,” he said. “Don’t jump on ​the first deal you see.”

data.title: Walmart stocks up on inflation-weary shoppers ahead of the holidays
data.description: Walmart isn’t just adding inventory for the holiday shopping season; it’s also racking up more customers looking for discounts as inflation maintains its grip on the U.S. economy. The retail giant on Thursday said it gained market share and raised its sales outlook for the third time this year as bargain hunters across income levels hit stores and fill their online shopping carts. “Looking ahead, we expect a strong holiday season,” CEO John Furner said on an earnings call with analysts Thursday. Walmart, which is generally considered a barometer for the U.S. economy, has long been a go-to store for consumers seeking discounts. Rising prices have pushed many consumers to rethink where they shop, and Walmart has benefited from more higher-income shoppers. As it draws more affluent customers, the company has launched a fashion-forward women’s apparel brand and expanded its e-commerce and advertising businesses. Walmart isn’t alone in gaining momentum with thrifty shoppers ahead of the holidays. Rivals Target and Costco are also seeing customers respond to their value offerings, both posting sales increases and Target raising its outlook. The results illustrate the resilience of American consumers, who keep spending even while grocery and gas prices rise and paycheck growth lags the pace of inflation. “In spite of that, consumers are finding ways to get what they need for their families,” Matthew Shay, president of the National Retail Federation, told NBC News on Wednesday. Still, it’s shaping up to be a strong holiday season, and not just for Walmart. The National Retail Federation forecasts that sales in November and December will top $1 trillion in the U.S. for the first time. But that doesn’t necessarily mean consumers are buying more items; rather, they’re paying a higher price at checkout. This season, Walmart said it lowered the price of 7,700 items by the end of the third quarter while expanding deals on groceries. The company said it will also offer a Thanksgiving meal basket for 10 at $3.50 per person, including turkey, Stove Top stuffing, mashed potatoes and other staples. Walmart also raked in more revenue from its membership fees, which surged 17% in the quarter. The company announced a bundled deal that includes memberships to Walmart+ and its warehouse-club subsidiary Sam’s Club, as well as perks including free access to streaming platforms and gas savings. While shoppers seem to be sold on Walmart heading into the holidays, Wall Street was a bit more cautious. The company’s stock slipped about 1% to $126 a share amid a broader market sell-off Thursday, even as quarterly revenue and profit surpassed investors’ expectations. Goldman Sachs analysts said they still rated Walmart’s stock a “buy,” projecting it’ll hit $132 a share. Nonetheless, they also flagged risks to the company’s outlook, including the potential for an economic slowdown and more intense price competition from its big-box and online rivals.

data.title: Outages impact Chase banking online and at some branches
data.description: An issue with Chase banking services led to some customers of that institution and others reporting trouble accessing their accounts and withdrawing funds Monday. The issues appeared to be affecting both online and in-person branch transactions. “Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” Chase said in a statement. “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.” The issues at Chase were caused by a “technical bug, not a cyber issue,” according to a source familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak publicly. A Zelle representative said that a technical issue on its platform originated with Chase. “This is a Chase issue,” a Zelle spokesman told NBC News. “You need to speak to them.” Reports began to surface online Monday afternoon from customers across a range of banks saying they were receiving error messages when attempting to perform bank transactions. The outages were the latest in a series of nationwide tech glitches over the past week. Microsoft Outlook went offline for approximately 48 hours last week due to what it called a capacity upgrade. On Friday, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for several hours over what U.S. officials said was a botched facilities upgrade.

data.title: How grocery prices have changed since Trump took office
data.description: Are President Donald Trump’s policies bringing down grocery bills? Grocery prices have been on the rise for most of the past six years, as the war in Iran, supply chain bottlenecks, the war in Ukraine and excessive profit-taking here in the U.S. have put a strain on consumers’ wallets. Trump campaigned heavily on the price of food in 2024, promising that if elected he would lower costs. Has that happened? To find out, NBC News is tracking the average grocery price of eggs, ground beef, and other common grocery-basket goods. The average price of eggs — a frequent stand-in for inflation during the campaign — have declined from a spring 2025 peak and are now down 31% since Trump took office last year. Average orange juice prices are up about 20% and ground beef prices are up about 15% from January 2025. Since 2021, NBC News has monitored the average point-of-sale price for eggs, chicken, bread, ground beef and other common grocery items. The graphic below shows their current average prices, along with how much those prices have changed since Trump took office in 2025. The grocery price data, provided by the global marketing research firm NIQ, is collected from real checkout prices paid nationwide at grocery stores, drugstores, mass merchandisers, selected dollar stores, selected warehouse clubs and military commissaries. The Bureau of Labor Statistics’ monthly consumer price index, which uses human data collectors and includes other food product categories, is another resource for average price data. This article will be updated twice each month.

data.title: Tracking U.S., state and county gas prices, in maps and charts
data.description: The war in Iran has led to higher prices at the gas pump. Gas prices in the United States, up by nearly 30% since the U.S. and Israel launched the war, have soared as the global oil supply constricts. Now at a national average of about $3.80 per gallon, according to data from motor club AAA, this price increase is straining already-stretched budgets in households across the country. NBC News is tracking gas prices and how they change at the national, state and county levels, and will be updating this article daily with the latest data. Average gas prices have increased more than a dollar since the U.S. and Israel first attacked Iran. In two states — California and Hawaii — average gas prices are at least $5 per gallon. Georgia, North Carolina and Texas are paying the least, according to AAA data. According to a Brown University analysis, the increase in gas prices since the start of the war has cost Americans more than $80 billion. Fuel costs aren’t limited to gas. Jet fuel prices have been surging as well, leading airlines to increase airfares. Oil prices have spiked, then see-sawed, were approaching pre-war levels, and are now surging again as turmoil in the Middle East continues.

data.title: Romanov sapphire worn by Russian empress fetches $4.9M at auction
data.description: A Romanov sapphire weighing nearly 198 carats on a diamond-covered bracelet sold for more than 4.1 million Swiss francs ($4.9 million) at auction, vastly higher than the expected price range, Sotheby’s said. The cushion-shaped sapphire attributed to onetime ownership of Russia’s imperial family was billed as a very rare stone, and had been expected to fetch between 850,000 and 1.7 million francs ($1 million and $2 million) at the Geneva auction late Wednesday. The buyer, a private collector, wasn’t identified. The 197.80-carat Ceylon sapphire likely came from the Mughal Empire in south Asia, made its way into Russia’s imperial jewels in the 19th century and is one of the most important surviving gemstones from the Russian court. Dowager Empress Maria Feodorovna, Czar Nicholas II’s mother, wore the sapphire at the Winter Palace Ball of 1903 — “widely regarded as the last great spectacle of Imperial Russia and immortalized in some of the most iconic images of the Romanov court,” the auction house said. After the Russian Revolution, the sapphire was recorded in inventory before entering the Soviet government’s dispersal sales of imperial treasures, Sotheby’s said.
